idiom_name: value struct + structured bindings over the owner's columns
implementation_notes: Without an ORM the value stays an aggregate struct with value semantics (which is already most of what the pattern wants) and the decompose/recompose pair is written by hand around whatever row abstraction the project uses. C++17 structured bindings make the recompose half a single declaration that names the columns' meanings, and the same aggregate initialization works in reverse for the write. Choose this over ODB when the project has no code generator or when the value is used in a handful of places; keep the column names in one helper per value type rather than repeating them per query.
pitfalls: A value type with a std::string member is not trivially copyable: never memcpy it into a row buffer, and keep the aggregate default-constructible only if the row API needs it.
Structured bindings name the columns positionally - swapping two columns of the same type compiles and silently corrupts both values; assert on the column list once per query.

variants.name: ODB composite value type (code-generated decompose/recompose)
variants.idiom_name: ODB #pragma db value composite value type mapped to the owner's columns
variants.implementation_notes: ODB is the C++ realization of the classic structure: a class annotated #pragma db value is a composite value type, i.e. a C++ type mapped to more than one database column, and the ODB compiler generates the decompose/recompose code that a hand-written mapper would otherwise need. The value has no object id (values have no identity) and no table; the #pragma db column specifier on the owning member supplies the column-name prefix, so the same value type can be embedded twice without a collision. Choose it when several value types are shared across many persistent classes - the generated code is where the duplication would otherwise live.
pitfalls: A composite value cannot carry an object id, and ODB generates its support code when the header declaring #pragma db value is compiled - putting the pragma in the wrong translation unit gives link errors rather than a mapping error.
The column prefix is set on the owning member, not on the value type: forgetting it when the type appears twice makes both occurrences map to the same columns.
